extracted.intended_audience: agency officials, administrative lawyers, judges, and legislators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and minimum legal standards for federal administrative agencies on hearings, evidence, decisionmaking, sanctions, licensing, examiners, records, judicial review, and construction/effect of the Administrative Procedure Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presiding officer powers and independent function
rubrics_metrics.description: Presiding officers shall perform a real function and independently exercise specified powers rather than serving merely as a notary or policeman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presiding officer "would have and should independently exercise all the powers numbered in the subsection." Agencies should not conduct hearings 'from behind the scenes' where they cannot know the detailed happenings in the hearing room and do not hear or see the private parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standard — relevant, reliable, and probative
rubrics_metrics.description: No sanction may be imposed or rule or order be issued except as supported by relevant, reliable, and probative evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While any evidence may be received, agencies are required to exclude irrelevant and unduly repetitious evidence. Standards and principles of probity and reliability prevailing in courts of law or equity should govern administrative proceedings, though exclusionary rules of evidence need not strictly apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — proponent bears burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as statutes otherwise provide, the proponent of a rule or order has the burden of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proponent must come forward with a prima facie case, and other parties advocating a different result also have a burden to maintain their positions. Agencies may not arbitrarily disbelieve credible and credited evidence; proponents of denial of relief must sustain such denial by the requisite kind and quality of contrary evidence. Agencies are not entitled to presume conduct unlawful absent prima facie showing by applicants where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation rights — oral, documentary, rebuttal, cross-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Any party may present his case or defense by oral or documentary evidence, submit rebuttal evidence, and conduct reasonable cross-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where necessary to bring out the truth, cross-examination should be afforded. Adequate opportunity must be provided to prepare and submit appropriate rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-evidence procedures for rulemaking and initial licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: In rule making or determining applications for initial licenses, the agency may adopt procedures for the submission of evidence in written form so far as the interest of any party will not be prejudiced thereby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written evidence provisions are designed for cases where submission is generally in written form; the practice must be limited to specified classes of cases and only where it does not prejudice any party. The right of cross-examination extends, in a proper case, to written evidence submitted pursuant to this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record of proceedings and official notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The record of evidence taken and papers filed is exclusive for decision and, upon payment of costs, is available to the parties. Where decision rests on official notice of a material fact not appearing in the evidence of record, any party may on timely request show the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When agencies take 'official notice' they must state it on the record or in their decisions and afford the parties an opportunity to show the contrary. The record is the basis for decision and must be available to parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial decisions, recommended decisions, and agency review
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the agency has not presided at reception of evidence, the presiding officer must make the initial decision unless the agency undertakes to make the initial decision. If the presiding officer makes the initial decision, it becomes the decision of the agency in the absence of appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agency makes the initial decision without having presided, the officer who took the evidence must first make a recommended decision (with exceptions in rulemaking/initial licenses where tentative decisions or omission of intermediate procedure may be allowed). Parties may agree to waive intermediate procedures. On appeal or review, the agency has all powers it would have had in making the initial decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submittals, proposed findings, exceptions, and supporting reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to each recommended or other decision or review the parties must be given an opportunity to submit (1) proposed findings and conclusions or (2) exceptions to recommended decisions or other decisions being appealed or reviewed, and (3) supporting reasons for such findings, conclusions, or exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Supporting reasons" means briefs on the law and facts must be received and fully considered by every recommending, deciding, or reviewing officer. They must also hear such oral argument as may be required by law. Where issues of fact are serious and the case becomes adversary in character, oral argument before all recommending, deciding, or reviewing officers should be provided as good practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required content of decisions — findings, conclusions, and basis
rubrics_metrics.description: All recommended or other decisions become part of the record and must include (1) findings and conclusions, as well as the basis therefor, upon all the material issues of fact, law, or discretion presented by the record and (2) the appropriate agency action or denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings and conclusions must be sufficiently related to the record to advise the parties of their record basis; statements of reasons may be long or short depending on complexity. Findings must include issues of administrative discretion as well as law and fact; credibility determinations should be made where oral testimony is conflicting and credibility is material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on agency powers and sanctions (jurisdictional constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sanction may not be imposed or substantive rule or order be issued except within the jurisdiction delegated to the agency and as authorized by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may not undertake anything statutes or other authority do not authorize. Specific grants cannot be stretched; general grants cannot be exercised beyond their generality. Agencies may not assume functions of another agency. Examples: an agency authorized only to issue cease-and-desist orders may not create a licensing system; a licensing authority may not assume to issue desist orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing procedures and revocation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are required, with due regard for rights of interested parties, to proceed with reasonable dispatch to conclude and decide proceedings on applications for licenses. They are not to withdraw a license without first giving the licensee notice in writing and an opportunity to demonstrate or achieve compliance, except in cases of willfulness or where public health, interest, or safety requires otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dispatch means proceed as rapidly as feasible and practicable. Undue delays are subject to correction by mandatory injunction. Exceptions to notice before revocation apply only where demonstrable facts fully and fairly warrant them; willfulness must be manifest. The 'public * * * interest' standard requires immediate action but does not permit arbitrary disregard of notice and opportunity. Temporary permits may be excepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of judicial review — who may seek review
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person suffering legal wrong because of any agency action, or adversely affected within the meaning of any statute, is entitled to judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase 'legal wrong' refers to illegal effects specified in subsection (e). The adverse effect must be an illegal effect, not merely an adverse personal effect. The relevant law includes constitutional and statutory law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form, venue, and prerequisites for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: The technical form of proceeding for judicial review is any special proceeding provided by statute or, absent or inadequate such procedure, any relevant form of legal action in any court of competent jurisdiction. Agency action is also made subject to judicial review in enforcement proceedings except to the extent that prior, adequate, and exclusive opportunity for such review is provided by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common-law actions (e.g., declaratory judgments) are operative where special statutory forms are lacking. Agencies may require by rule an appeal to superior agency authority before judicial review only where the administrative decision meanwhile is inoperative; rules cannot force exhaustion while the administrative action remains effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim relief and preservation of status quo pending review
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending judicial review any agency may postpone the effective date of its action. Upon conditions and as may be necessary to prevent irreparable injury, any reviewing court may postpone the effective date of any agency action or preserve the status quo pending conclusion of review proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and agencies may use equitable authority to prevent irreparable injury or to afford parties an adequate judicial remedy; this does not permit courts to grant initial licenses but provides intermediate relief to make judicial review effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of review and categories of unlawful agency action
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing courts must decide relevant questions of law, interpret constitutional and statutory provisions, and determine the meaning or applicability of any agency action. They must (A) compel action unlawfully withheld or unreasonably delayed and (B) hold unlawful any action, findings, or conclusions found to be (1) arbitrary, (2) contrary to the Constitution, (3) contrary to statutes or short of statutory right, (4) without observance of procedure required by law, (5) unsupported by substantial evidence upon the administrative record where hearings are authorized by sections 7 and 8, or (6) unwarranted by the facts so far as the latter are subject to trial de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In making these determinations courts consider the whole record or such parts cited by the parties, and due account must be taken of the rule of prejudicial error. 'Finding' and 'conclusion' include failures to find or conclude as required by law and the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial-evidence standard
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Substantial evidence' means evidence which on the whole record is clearly substantial, sufficient to support a finding or conclusion under section 7(c), and material to the issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must exercise independent judgment to determine whether, on the whole record, the evidence is sufficiently substantial to support agency findings. Agencies have the initial function to determine sufficiency and must undertake that inquiry carefully and dispassionately. Reliance upon suspicion, surmise, implications, or plainly incredible evidence is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners — appointment, qualifications, rotation, tenure, and compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are required to appoint such examiners as may be necessary for proceedings under sections 7 and 8, who are to be assigned to cases in rotation so far as practicable and to perform no inconsistent duties. They are removable only for good cause determined by the Civil Service Commission after opportunity for hearing and upon the record thereof. They are to receive compensation prescribed by the Commission independently of agency recommendations or ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Civil Service Commission must fix appropriate qualifications; agencies should seek qualified and competent persons. The Commission must afford any examiner an opportunity for a hearing before acceding to an agency request for removal; the hearing and decision would be made under sections 7 and 8. Rotation prevents disfavoring examiners by rendering them inactive. Compensation and classification are to be set independently by the Commission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction, constitutional protection, severability, and effective dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the bill is to diminish constitutional rights or limit or repeal additional requirements of law. The unconstitutionality of any portion or application of the bill is not to affect other portions or applications. Agencies are granted all authority necessary to comply with the bill. The bill would become law three months after approval except that sections 7 and 8 take effect six months after approval, the requirements of section 11 become effective a year after approval, and no requirement is mandatory as to any agency proceeding initiated prior to the effective date of such requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and limitations must be interpreted and applied by agencies in the first instance but enforcement and final interpretation is a function of reviewing courts. 'Initiated' means a proceeding formally begun (e.g., issuance of a complaint or notice of a rule-making hearing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency responsibility and need for vigilant enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must make the first, primary, and most far-reaching effort to comply with the terms and spirit of the bill; judicial review is indispensable but will operate in relatively few cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must prevent avoidance of requirements by indirection and determine meaning of words and phrases (e.g., 'good cause'). Cause must be real and demonstrable; findings required by the bill must be sustainable on inquiry by a reviewing court. If provisions fail to operate as intended, supplemental legislation may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and cautions regarding exemptions (rulemaking and initial licenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The exemption of rule making and determining initial applications for licenses from provisions of sections 5(c), 7(c), and 8(a) may require change if too broad; where cases present sharply contested issues of fact, agencies should not take advantage of the exemptions as a matter of good practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The committee notes these exemptions are broadly drawn to simplify the bill but cautions agencies should adopt intermediate recommended decision procedures when issues of fact are sharply controverted or accusatory in nature.
